title: "Design Lab: A Durable Distributed Message Queue in Go"

# Design Lab: A Durable Distributed Message Queue in Go

[Queue workers](153-queue-workers-backpressure.qmd) consume work. This lab investigates the broker behind them: persistent partitions, producer acknowledgments, consumer offsets, and recovery. Build a single-node append log first; replication is a separate milestone with an explicit correctness argument.

## Define the contract

Use `Append(ctx, partition, key, payload)` to return an offset and `Fetch(ctx, partition, offset, maxBytes)` to read a bounded batch. Ordering exists within one partition. Hash the customer key to preserve that customer's order; do not promise ordering across partitions.

| Record | Fields |
|--------|--------|
| Log entry | partition, offset, key, length, payload, checksum |
| Consumer checkpoint | group, partition, next offset, owner generation |
| Producer dedupe state | producer identity, epoch, last sequence, prior result |

The initial contract is at-least-once delivery. A consumer commits its next offset after a successful durable effect. A crash between effect and checkpoint causes replay; make the effect idempotent in the same database transaction as its dedupe marker.

## Build the broker in Go

1. Use one bounded append channel and one log-writer goroutine per partition. Assign offsets in that goroutine, outside HTTP handler scheduling order.
2. Frame records with length and checksum, enforce a maximum frame size, and handle short writes. Acknowledge according to a written policy: OS-buffered versus file-synced durability are different promises.
3. Recover on restart by scanning valid frames. A torn final frame can be truncated; unexpected corruption in the middle requires a reported recovery failure.
4. Expose bounded long polling with request contexts. Cap outstanding fetches and bytes per batch. Persist checkpoints independently of client connections.
5. Add group ownership generations. Reject checkpoint updates from an old generation after rebalance; cancel its worker and handle already-running effects with durable deduplication or fencing.

A Go interface sketch for the consumer boundary is:

```go
type Delivery struct {
	Partition int
	Offset    int64
	Body      []byte
}

type Consumer interface {
	Fetch(context.Context, int) ([]Delivery, error)  // byte budget
	Commit(context.Context, int, int64, int64) error // partition, next offset, generation
}
```

Imports and broker implementation are exercises. A channel carries work inside the broker; the log provides restart survival. Review the [WAL chapter](../17-systems-programming/142b-write-ahead-log.qmd) for framing and recovery mechanics.

## Replication changes acknowledgment

For the next milestone, describe leader election, leader epochs, committed offsets, follower catch-up, and the rule preventing an old leader from accepting authoritative writes. A majority of arbitrary disk writes without an agreed log order is not a consensus protocol. Use a proven replicated-log implementation if you need these guarantees beyond the lab.

Retention must account for consumer lag. If a checkpoint falls behind the earliest retained offset, return an explicit reset-required error. Do not silently advance it. A partition-count increase can change key placement and per-key ordering unless migration is coordinated.

Kafka's [design documentation](https://kafka.apache.org/41/design/design/) is a reference for partition and delivery concepts, not a claim that this small broker reproduces Kafka.

## Failure evidence

Kill the broker before and after sync, lose the producer response, restart the consumer after its database commit, and rebalance during a long-running job. Record acknowledged offsets, recovered offsets, duplicate effects, and rejected stale checkpoints. Test disk-full errors and a consumer slower than retention. The passing result preserves the declared durability policy and produces at most one logical database effect per message despite duplicate delivery.

Compare this lab with the [notification](../99-projects/101-system-design/02-notification-delivery.qmd) and [click aggregation](../99-projects/101-system-design/11-click-event-aggregation.qmd) projects: the same log serves different replay and ordering needs.
